# Authoring hard agent-benchmark tasks

> **Which file am I?** The `AGENTS.md` entry point, read automatically by OpenAI Codex,
> Google Antigravity, and other AGENTS.md-aware agents. Cursor reads the same knowledge
> from `.cursor/rules/`; Claude Code from `SKILL.md`. All of them are generated from one
> source — edit `SKILL.md` or `references/`, then run `python scripts/port.py`.

Everything below applies whenever you are designing, building, critiquing or debugging a
Terminal-Bench 2 / Harbor benchmark task.


This skill packages what was measured across 30+ Terminal-Bench 2 task slots — the ones that
cleared a difficulty gate, and the many that died first. It exists because the intuition
almost everyone brings to "write a hard task" is wrong in a specific, repeatable way, and
the correction is cheap once you know it.

## New here? Fifteen minutes, in this order

**1 · Read "The one law" and the kill-list below (5 min).** Do not skip to the reference
files. If you internalise only one thing, make it the pre-build test: *what must the agent
build that the verifier could not hand it by simulating?*

**2 · Set up retrieval (1 min).** The field manual is ~35k tokens and will not fit in one
read call. Index it once and query it instead — this is the difference between a design
question costing ~1k tokens and ~35k:

```bash
python scripts/dr.py index --no-embed
python scripts/dr.py ask "what trips ava_review verifier_coverage" --fast
```

**3 · Put a board up (1 min).** Before you write anything, see where your slots actually
stand — and specifically which review stage each one is sitting at:

```bash
python scripts/taskdesk.py --org <your-task-org>
```

**4 · Then, when you have a slot to work:** `references/ci-stages.md` before your first push
(it is the difference between one three-hour CI run and three of them), and the phase table
below for everything else.

**The two mistakes that cost the most, stated once so you can avoid both:** designing a task
where the agent *checks* a property instead of *constructing* an object, and treating CI as a
test loop instead of a confirmation step.

## The one law

**The gate does not measure how hard your task was to build. It measures whether strong
agents, handed every rule in fair prose, still fail to CONSTRUCT a correct artifact.**

Everything else in this skill is downstream of three consequences:

**1. A property the agent CHECKS cannot carry difficulty; only an object the agent must
CONSTRUCT can.** The pre-build test: *what must the agent build that the verifier could not
hand it by simulating?* If the honest answer is "nothing — it just has to decide a predicate
correctly", the design is dead, however subtle that predicate looks to a human.

**2. Knowing N is not achieving N.** Print the closed-form optimum in the spec. Constructing
a legal object that attains it is the hard part. Hiding the number makes the task unfair,
not hard.

**3. Fairness forces every graded rule into agent-visible text.** The only thing you may
withhold is the *consequence* of the rules taken together. State premises, never inferences.
Performing the derivation for the agent in prose costs roughly 3 of 5 trials — measured.

The failure this skill exists to prevent: a week spent on an exotic semantics, agents solve
it 2/2 in under an hour, and the report says the difficulty crux was never reached. That is
not bad luck. It is one of a small number of measurably dead shapes.

## Before designing anything: run the kill-list

All thirteen shapes below are dead on measurement, not theory. Numbering matches
`references/hardness-laws.md` §3.1, where each row carries its evidence and evidence class.
Killing a design here costs a few thousand tokens; killing it in CI costs a day.

Four rows (✅) have a **measured repair mechanism** — a real recipe at the cited section. The
other nine (⛔) are shapes to abandon: no known rescue, and the constructive move is to pick a
proven floor shape from §3.2 instead.

| # | Dead shape | The tell | Repair |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Checked predicate** | The core is "decide whether X holds" — static analysis, type/alias/escape inference, "does a legal X exist?" | ✅ **Add a constructive leg** — the agent must build an object a wrong belief renders illegal → **§5.1** (carries a same-slot positive control) |
| 2 | **Factorising legality** | Admission is a conjunction of independent per-field conditions, so the agent probes one coordinate at a time. | ✅ **Union of boxes** — one shared pool, so per-field probing is wrong in *both* directions → **§5.2**. Or move difficulty onto **computed object identity** → §5.2 end |
| 3 | **Product of per-item ranges** | Items just occupy positions under a cumulative resource. Solver bait — `allow_internet` is mandated, so the agent installs OR-Tools. | ✅ **State graph reached by destructive moves**. Cheap tell: *what does a move destroy?* → **§3.1**, in the prose below the table. Escape hatch: feasible density below ~1e-7 |
| 7 | **Breadth of independent one-line rules** | Many clean rules × many records. Volume mistaken for depth. | ✅ **Coupling repair** — each stage *consumes* context so selection is a fold; one slip shifts everything downstream. One SPEC sentence → **§3.1**, in the prose below the table. Anti-pattern: a cumulative archive silently neutralises it |
| 4 | **Optimization margin** | "Get within X% of optimal." | ⛔ Agents land on or near optimal routinely. Needs a second scarce resource — rebuild from §3.2 |
| 5 | **Named crux / library-returned object** | The crux has a name in the literature, or a library call returns the load-bearing object. | ⛔ That is knowledge, not difficulty. Replace the core |
| 6 | **Fully-specified custom-semantics interpreter** | "The API is the spec itself." | ⛔ Transcription. Measured 4/4 solved on a probe rig |
| 8 | **Scale / brute-force thesis** | "Make the state space bigger." | ⛔ Two correct solvers agree at any size; the agent writes a second and cross-checks |
| 9 | **Blindness engineering** | Hoping the agent can't verify itself. | ⛔ A spec complete enough to be *fair* is self-verifiable. Partly superseded: the gap opens when the spec is sufficient AND the answer is a constructed artifact meeting a printed optimum |
| 10 | **Rare deciding rules** | A clause that rarely fires. | ⛔ Invisible in the evidence means invisible in the result |
| 11 | **Order-independent end state** | Every correct plan reaches the same end state. | ⛔ A fatal move strands something immediately, so backtracking is free. Needs a wrong move that is unrecoverable AND not locally visible |
| 12 | **Tightness as the sole defense** | "The feasible fraction is tiny." | ⛔ Worth zero between 1e-4 and 1e-1; only below ~1e-7 counts |
| 13 | **Trap aimed at one algorithm** | The trap catches minimax but not BFS. | ⛔ A different standard algorithm sidesteps it |

There is a fifth repair that does not appear above because it is not a *shape* fix at all:
when your design survives the whole kill-list but the shipped instances were simply too kind,
rebuild the **data** rather than the semantics → **§6.4**. It is the only repair that leaves
your core intact.

### Translating your domain into a row

Rows are stated structurally, so the mapping from what you actually built is a real
inferential step. The most common benchmark domains and where they land:

| If you built… | Look hard at | Note |
|---|---|---|
| A **scheduler / planner** (jobs, machines, makespan, dependencies) | **#3** — jobs occupying time slots *is* a product of per-item ranges, and RCPSP/job-shop is also **#5** (named crux; CP-SAT returns the object) | The single most common shape authors write, and one of the deadest |
| A **validator / linter / classifier** over records | **#1**, and **#2** if the rules are per-field | |
| A **many-rules pipeline** (N rules × M items) | **#7** | Has a real repair — the coupling fix |
| An **"optimize this" task** | **#4** *only if* you grade a margin ("within X%") | If you print the exact optimum and grade attainment, that is the *winning* skeleton (§3.2), not #4. These two read alike and mean opposite things. |
| A **parser / interpreter** for a custom format | **#6** | |

Two laws bite hardest on resource-and-optimum designs and are easy to miss because they live
outside §3: **"you can force a WALK, you cannot force a MARGIN"** (§5.5 — move-attached
divergence can be forced onto every legal path by construction; resource-level divergence
cannot, and was measured dead at *both* tightness settings), and the companion warning that
**ordering is always cheap** — always restart-repairable and always audited by a printed N,
so difficulty spent on sequencing alone refunds itself.

Three more failure modes are not on the numbered list but kill just as reliably: **naming
instead of legality** (a wrong belief that only *misnames* something), **a cap nothing rises
toward** (two populations moving monotonically apart, so contention never occurs), and a
**self-cancelling rule** (one that lowers demand on the very resource your floor is defined
on). Also read §3.1's *"refutation must be SHARED and LATE"* — a wrong choice refuted
locally costs the agent one retry, which is no cost at all.

When a design survives all of this, red-team it against two or three alternatives before
building. Kill for tokens, not build-hours.

`references/hardness-laws.md` is the substance of this skill; the rest is scaffolding to make
it cheap to apply. It is ~35k tokens and **will not fit in one read call** — plan on two, or
jump to the section you need via its table of contents.

## The workflow, and where to look at each phase

Load the reference for the phase you are in rather than reading everything up front.

```
claim  →  read sub-category off the PLATFORM (it is not in the repo)
       →  check similarity denominator (same-author, same-sub-category)
       →  red-team 3+ designs against the kill-list
       →  proposal (4-section house format, zero internal lore)
       →  build
       →  FULL LOCAL PIPELINE GREEN
       →  preflight
       →  ONE push
       →  read the gate arithmetic, not just the label
```

(the prose artifacts are human-written; your role there is outline, critique, red-team —

## Finishing faster: the gate is not the only thing that blocks you

A full review run takes **about three hours** across 17 stages, and **a block at any early
stage skips every stage downstream — including `trials`.** So a failure in a five-minute prose
field does not cost you a checkbox; it costs you the whole difficulty measurement, and you
learn that three hours later.

The measured case: one slot needed **three CI runs, and neither of the first two failures was
about difficulty.** Run 1 died on `ava_review` → `verifier_coverage` (a reference solution that
could exit nonzero on a path the shipped set never reaches). Run 2 died on a re-roll of
`difficulty_explanation_quality` (a graded prose field that never named a real-world
audience). Both were checkable locally in minutes. Both threw away a full difficulty
measurement.

So the fastest route to a cleared slot is not a better task — it is **one push that clears all
17 stages**. Three habits get you there:

- **Run the free rubric self-grade before every push.** All 31 criteria ship in your own repo
  at `<your-task-repo>/dynamo-rubric.toml` — **not** in this skill, with full guidance text. No API key needed. Grade
  yourself as an explicit PASS/FAIL/NA table with a one-line reason per criterion — every
  rubric failure in this corpus landed in one of the four graded prose fields.
- **Check the four blockers preflight does not catch** — they are listed with their fixes in
  `references/ci-stages.md`, and each one has cost somebody a full cycle.
- **Once a run is green, stop pushing.** The LLM stages are non-deterministic: identical text
  passed `review` on one run and failed it on the next. And never push mid-flight — per-PR
  concurrency cancels the run you are waiting on.

Read `references/ci-stages.md` in full before your first push. It is the difference between
one three-hour run and three of them.

## Two steps people skip, and what they cost

**Read the sub-category off the platform.** The GitHub repo is boilerplate until you build
it — the assigned sub-category lives only on the platform board, and it determines your
entire kill-list and your similarity risk. Guessing it wastes a design.

**Get the full local pipeline green BEFORE the one push.** Not "tests pass". Specifically:
every archetype in your battery dies *through the shipped verifier*; a blind solver written
from the spec prose alone agrees with your reference; a three-way fuzz finds zero
divergences; the reference runs well inside the disclosed cap. Every push re-rolls the
LLM-graded stages, so a one-line fix costs the same wall-clock as a redesign.

Then run `scripts/preflight.py <task-dir>` (needs Python 3.11+; use `py -3.12` on
Windows where `python` is older). It catches format and config failures that would otherwise
burn a full CI cycle.

## You already shipped, and agents solved it

This is the most common expensive state, so handle it before anything else.

**Step zero — check the arithmetic, then read `difficulty_crux`.** Both take under a minute
and together they decide which repair you need.

*The arithmetic first,* because it is routinely misread. The gate needs **≤ 2/5 solved**, AND
**good-valid-fail + soft-timeout ≥ 3**, AND **≥ 1 good-valid-fail** — see §2. There is no
partial credit. "Three agents did fail" sounds like a near miss and usually is not: 3/5 solved
means you are over the solve bar *and* short on the fail bar simultaneously. Know which of the
two bars you missed before designing a fix, because they point at different repairs.

*Then `difficulty_crux` on the failing trials* — the single most diagnostic field in the report:

- **`NA`** — agents never reached the decision point you designed; they solved it by a route
  that bypassed your crux. This is the fingerprint of a dead **shape**. Go to the kill-list
  above; no amount of instance tuning will help.
- **`PASS`** — agents reached your crux and it bit. Your shape *may* be alive, and this is the
  profile the data-only rebuild (§6.4) is for. **But PASS is necessary, not sufficient:** run
  the kill-list anyway before reaching for §6.4. A design that lands on a kill-list row cannot
  be repaired with data, and rebuilding instances against a shape an off-the-shelf solver eats
  costs you a full CI cycle to learn nothing.
- **`FAIL` on a failing trial** — that failure was carried by a task defect rather than your
  crux, so the fail is spurious. Fix the defect before believing any of the numbers (§9.1).

Then three facts, in this order:

**1. A 2/2 solved is authoritative and final.** The evidence is asymmetric: a *blocked* result
is weak evidence a design is wrong (at n=5 against a 60% bar, a genuinely 70%-fail design
still misses about 16% of the time), but a *solved* result is strong evidence it is too easy.
Two independent 2/2 on one skeleton is conclusive. Do not argue with it.

**2. Stop running it today.** The stop condition is 2/2 → stop the same day; the hard ceiling
is two runs per twelve hours on one design. Re-rolling is how people spend a week confirming
something they already knew.

**3. The fix is structural, never quantitative.** These are all measured waste after a 2/2:
adding more rules, adding more records, growing the state space, cutting spec prose, or
hiding a rule (QC blocks that as hidden knowledge). De-disclosure cannot rescue a design with
no structural leg — one slot cut inference sentences *and* added a belief family and went 2/2
again, with agents merely taking longer.

Then find your design's row in the kill-list above and follow the cited § for its mechanism.
`references/hardness-laws.md` §9.2 has the same four measured 2/2 → 0/5 repairs as a table
routed to their mechanism sections — use whichever entry point you reached first.

**The one-hour experiment that decides shape-dead vs instances-too-kind.** Before committing
to either branch, measure rather than argue. Install the obvious off-the-shelf solver for your
domain and run it on your sealed instances at the disclosed cap — that is what a gate agent
will literally do. Alongside it, run the **one-line-policy battery** (§3.1): write the three
most obvious greedy policies and enumerate the true optimum exactly on small instances.
Winners should sit near zero.

If the solver reaches the target inside the cap, or any one-liner wins more than about 20%,
the shape is dead and no data rebuild will save it. If both sit near zero, your instances were
the problem and §6.4 is the right repair. Methodology warning from §3.1, learned expensively:
it took four attempts to get one of those numbers right and every wrong one was plausible —
use full enumeration on small instances, never a pruned search you wrote yourself, and never
infer hardness from a search-cost ratio.

### A worked repair, end to end

The corpus's sharpest A/B, because only the *requirement* changed — same fiction, same
artifact, same floor, same grading, same instance generator (§5.2):

**Before (2/2 solved, `difficulty_crux = NA`).** Disjoint per-register banks made admission
exactly a conjunction of independent per-field equalities. The cheapest route was to probe
one field at a time — about 18 decodes, 0.31 s against the reference's 0.16 s. A 2× ratio,
which no timeout, instance scaling or length change can ever separate. The exactness proof
had been recorded as a win; the proof *was* the leak.

**After (0/5 solved · 5 good-valid-fails · avg@5 0.000).** The disjoint banks were replaced
with **one shared pool**, making the admissible entry state a *union of boxes*. Per-field
probing is now wrong in both directions — it accepts configurations that grade wrong and
rejects valid ones. A single symbolic pass is also wrong: it derives only the archive's own
box, which is exactly what the old reference computed. The union stays exactly computable in
a bounded number of cheap passes, so exactness survives. Three of five gate agents
independently converged on the precise failure archetype the task named as its crux.

The transferable move: **the property you chose to make your floor provably exact is often
the very thing that makes it cheaply measurable.** When your exactness proof feels easy, run
the factorising test immediately — take the true configuration, change one field, and see
whether the graded property moves. If iterating that over each field reconstructs the whole
constraint, the difficulty was gone before you wrote a line.

## Reading a result honestly

A pass@ line is only ever true of **one head SHA**. Record the SHA next to the number, and
verify from the PR before acting on it — a slot filed as "blocked" from a superseded run has
cost real work more than once.

The gate is partly a **classification** problem, not only a difficulty problem. A genuinely
hard task can be blocked because trials ran out of agent clock mid-debug, and in-progress
timeouts count for neither side of the arithmetic. If your crux is *implementation volume* —
a multi-stage derivation the agent must code before it can test anything — you are exposed.
The fix is to cut implementation volume, never the semantic core. `references/rules/10-hardness-gate.md`
has the arithmetic.

Also: the rubric grader is non-deterministic. The same task scores differently across
pushes. Do not tune against a single roll.

## Separate the graded artifact from your thinking

The proposal goes through a rubric grader that penalises results-based framing. So the
proposal carries **zero** internal vocabulary — no pass@ numbers, no "archetype",
no "kill-list", no "we measured". All of that goes in a *separate* design record
(`design-<slug>.md`) that nobody grades, and which is where the red-team table, the measured
bars and the honest bet belong.

`assets/proposal-template.md` has the four-section house format and a grep check to run
before handing the proposal over. Use it — the format is mechanical and the points are free.

## Working several slots at once

One slot, one session. A session that owns one task cannot accidentally push another's repo
or blur two designs together. `assets/slot-session-prompt.md` is the handoff prompt;
`assets/batch-brief-template.md` is the shared brief to write *once per batch, before
spawning anything*, so parallel sessions stay consistent without talking to each other.

The brief matters most when two live slots share a sub-category: whichever opens a PR first
becomes the other's similarity denominator, so assign disjoint territories before either
session starts, and make them binding.

## Bundled tools

| Script | What it does | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `scripts/preflight.py` | Local gate check before pushing | Python 3.11+ (`tomllib`). `--probe` runs a live agent probe if configured. |
| `scripts/dr.py` | **Retrieval over this skill and your notes** — answers a design question in ~1–2k tokens instead of the ~35k a full read of the field manual costs | **Set this up first:** `python scripts/dr.py index --no-embed`, then `python scripts/dr.py ask "<question>" --fast`. Works immediately on the skill's own references — no notes, no API key, no model download. Needs `numpy`. → `references/retrieval.md` |
| `scripts/taskdesk.py` | **Board dashboard** — sweeps your task org and shows, per slot, which review stage it is sitting at and what it needs from you | `python scripts/taskdesk.py --org <your-org>` (or set `BENCH_ORG`). Needs `gh` authenticated. Read-only — it never pushes. |
| `scripts/session_desk.py` | Dashboard over your Claude Code sessions: live sessions, token spend, per-project activity | `python scripts/session_desk.py`. Writes `session-desk.html` beside itself. |

### The two desks

They answer different questions and cross-link to each other and back to this skill.

**Task desk** (`taskdesk.py`) — *where does the work stand?* One card per slot with a
stage-by-stage strip: green for passed, red for the stage that blocked you, amber for what is
running. Because an early block skips everything downstream, knowing you stopped at `review`
rather than at `trials` tells you immediately whether you are five minutes or a redesign away.
It sorts blocked slots first, and its action band names the fix for each.

**Session desk** (`session_desk.py`) — *what is this costing?* Live sessions, token spend by
day and by project, and a searchable ledger of past sessions. Useful when you are running
several slots in parallel and want to see where the budget actually went.

**Keeping them live.** Each page carries a meta-refresh, but that only re-reads the file — it
does **not** regenerate it, so on its own the refresh shows the same numbers forever. Use
watch mode, which is what actually rebuilds:

```bash
python scripts/session_desk.py --watch 60     # rebuild every 60s
python scripts/taskdesk.py --org <org> --watch # rebuild every 600s (gh is slow)
```

For Claude Code, a `SessionStart` hook running `session_desk.py --hook` keeps it current
without a loop.

**Which tools the session desk can see.** Claude Code (full transcripts with per-message
usage) and Codex (`~/.codex/sessions/**`, rollout files with running token totals). Rows are
tagged by source. **Cursor and Antigravity are not supported and this is deliberate** —
Cursor's workspaceStorage holds UI state with no token accounting, and Antigravity stores
protobuf; neither exposes a transcript that could be reported honestly, so the desk does not
guess at one. The task desk is tool-independent: it reads GitHub, so it works the same
everywhere.

## Honest limits

The laws carry evidence classes for a reason: **measured-gate** claims survived the
platform's own pass@ measurement; **design-kill** and **prospective** ones did not. Weight
them accordingly.

This is one author's corpus, and at n=5 against a 60% bar, a genuinely 70%-fail design still
misses the gate about 16% of the time — so a single blocked result is weak evidence that a
design is wrong, while a "too easy" result is strong evidence that it is. Treat the
asymmetry seriously: probe-dead does not mean gate-dead, but solved-2/2 really does mean
too easy.

Category-specific hazards (exact integers in scientific and geometric work; everything being
pre-named in low-level work; the correct-rules trap in games) are noted throughout
`references/hardness-laws.md`, but your sub-category distribution will differ. The
cross-cutting laws should transfer; the category briefs may not.
